title: Sri Lanka must prove recovery is more than a cycle: Hosking | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:00
-     - 18

By Devan Daniel 

Sri Lanka’s recovery has earned the patience of one of its most committed foreign investors, who continues to add to his holdings, but not yet his full conviction.

Hosking Partners LLP Founder and Portfolio Manager Jeremy Hosking said the London-based fund, encouraged by the 2027 Budget, would stay invested in Sri Lanka. He said it would make a substantially larger commitment only if the country proved its turnaround was secular rather than cyclical, a test he said entrenched resistance to change would make hard to pass.

“I think if we got more confidence that the Sri Lankan story was a secular story, we would increase our investments. That would imply quite a lot of change. I think the Government is pretty sound, but so is the resistance to change,” Hosking told the Daily FT during a visit to Sri Lanka.

Sri Lanka accounts for about 2% of the fund’s global portfolio, spread across about 12 companies. That is a large position for a global generalist in a frontier market outside the index. The fund added to its holdings when the economy collapsed in 2022, consistent with the capital cycle approach Hosking helped pioneer in 1986. The approach holds that returns recover where capital has fled and competition has thinned, and fall where capital floods in. Those holdings have since risen sharply.

“I think recent evidence, not least in your Budget, is quite encouraging, so we’ll be holding on for the time being,” he said, adding that the Government’s drive to widen the tax base and improve transparency was “very, very encouraging”.

Hosking’s prescription for lasting change starts with money. He said he would like Sri Lanka to adopt a currency board, and would prefer it to go further and dollarise.

“I don’t think the Sri Lankan rupee really merits its perpetuation as a currency,” he said, arguing that it had caused a misallocation of investment.

Foreign exchange controls, he said, block capital in both directions. Portfolio and corporate investors would like stakes in Sri Lankan businesses, while local investors want to invest abroad. He said capital must be free to leave if it is to come in, and that the controls invite the very abuse they are meant to prevent.

He said the appeal of interventionist economics lay in the power it confers, while its unintended consequences were generally negative. “Controlling the money supply to get the inflation rate down is not a job for 10,000 civil servants. It’s a job for a committee of about three people meeting once a month at most,” he said.

The second obstacle, Hosking said, is fragmentation, which is most acute in banking. Sri Lanka has too many banks, and the Central Bank micromanages them. He cited Nations Trust Bank (NTB), which he said was required to raise capital after acquiring an HSBC business in Sri Lanka last year.

“They’ve basically been punished for having the temerity to try and start consolidating the sector, which has far too many banks in it to begin with,” he said.

He also questioned the 10% cap on bank ownership, saying the fund favours anchor shareholders who care about long-term outcomes. “Insisting on a banking sector that is wholly in the hands of paid staff may not be the best outcome,” he said.

Consolidation, he said, is almost always the route to higher returns, and he pointed to the telecom merger in which the fund is a major shareholder. “Less competition tends to mean higher returns, and the Dialog share price has gone up five times. So we need more of that,” he said.

He likened Sri Lanka’s conglomerates, each with near-identical hotel and retail arms, to Hong Kong’s family groups, which each set up mobile phone subsidiaries and took decades of low returns to unwind.

Hosking said Sri Lanka’s struggle to attract capital was not entirely its own fault, but that its companies did not help themselves. “My industry, the fund management industry, is particularly dysfunctional, especially at this time. So it’s hard for a country like Sri Lanka and its companies to attract attention to themselves, but they don’t help themselves,” he said.

Global managers typically hold about 40 stocks, which in practice leaves Sri Lanka with no place in their portfolios, he said. Local companies compound this with weak investor relations, and the Government with a “siege mentality”. Hosking Partners gets around the problem by holding about 400 stocks, an approach he called “deeply unfashionable”.

CT Smith Securities Consultant and CT Holdings Director Marianne Page, who accompanied Hosking, said bank valuations had fallen from about 2.0 times book value a decade or more ago to about single digit levels. She said the Central Bank had urged consolidation for some 30 years without a single merger among the country’s 13 local commercial banks, and that leading conglomerates could combine their fragmented hotel businesses into a single investable company.

Globally, Hosking said the US was more likely mid-cycle than late-cycle. The fund remains wary of AI, where capital is pouring in on a scale he called “truly stupendous”, though it has profited from semiconductors and disc drives, the “picks and shovels” of the boom.

“This is going to be a huge stress test of the capital cycle lens,” he said.

title: Hosking Partners  ups Sri Lanka  exposure with  Rs. 1 b JAT stake | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:30
-     - 9

UK-based global equity investment manager Hosking Partners LLP has increased its exposure to Sri Lankan equities with the purchase of a 5.18% stake in JAT Holdings PLC for Rs. 1.05 billion. It bought the entire holding of the company’s second-largest shareholder, Falcon Trading Ltd.

Funds managed by Hosking Partners bought 27,077,498 shares at Rs. 38.8 each. Before the sale, Falcon Trading ranked second only to Aelian Gunawardene, who holds a controlling 63.63% stake in JAT.

The deal adds JAT to a Sri Lankan portfolio that Hosking Partners built largely during the 2023 economic crisis, which made it one of the country’s largest foreign equity investors. The firm is among the top 20 shareholders in John Keells Holdings, Aitken Spence, CT Holdings, Richard Pieris, Bukit Darah, Dialog Axiata, Tokyo Cement, Ceylon Guardian Investment Trust, Teejay Lanka and Lion Brewery. Its Sri Lankan equity portfolio was reported to exceed $ 60 million.

Hosking Partners was founded in 2013 by British investor Jeremy Hosking. It had approximately $ 7.55 billion in assets under management as at 30 September, 2026, according to its fund factsheet. It invests in international equity markets through institutional mandates and pooled investment funds. The firm takes a long-term, contrarian approach and uses capital-cycle analysis, which assesses how changes in supply within an industry affect companies’ returns on capital over time.

JAT Holdings is a Sri Lankan multinational with market-leading positions in industrial wood coatings in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Its acquisition of New Zealand-based Mirotone has expanded the Group’s international manufacturing and commercial presence, including in Australasia.

In the six months to 30 September, 2026, JAT’s Group revenue grew by 36% year-on-year, revenue from foreign operations rose by 115% and Group profit after tax increased by 27%. The company reported net assets of Rs. 23.48 a share as at that date.

title: Zero FDI, bitumen crunch stall urban and road capex; BOI to screen UDA investors | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:25
-     - 7

Sectoral Oversight Committee on Infrastructure and Strategic Development Chairman SJB MP S.M. Marikkar

The Board of Investment (BOI) is to take over financial screening of investors for State land from the Urban Development Authority (UDA) as it has failed to bring in any of the $ 500 million in foreign investment targeted for 2026, while a bitumen shortage caused by the West Asia conflict has capped road construction.

These were revealed during a session of the Parliamentary Sectoral Oversight Committee on Infrastructure and Strategic Development on Wednesday (18).

UDA Chairman M.G. Hemachandra said a Cabinet paper was moving forward to hand investor screening to the BOI. The UDA would then focus only on releasing land. “Previously, two places were checking the investor’s financial capability, both us and the BOI, so we submitted a Cabinet paper to hand that task to the BOI,” he said.

UDA officials admitted that none of the $ 500 million pledged for 2026 had materialised. They blamed the West Asia conflict for the cancellation of a planned investment forum in the Middle East.

Committee Chair SJB MP S.M. Marikkar pointed out that Port City had held its own investment forum in Dubai. He argued that forums held in Sri Lanka draw middlemen rather than genuine foreign capital. “Instead of attracting real investors, it looked like you were going to attract brokers, because investors do not come from inside Sri Lanka,” he said.

The UDA will also launch a public website listing available State land, zoning rules and master plan details, so that foreign investors can review opportunities before visiting Sri Lanka.

The conflict has also hit road construction. Road Development Authority (RDA) officials told the committee the agency could not reach full progress this year without bitumen. It is now aiming for 75% by year-end.

Sri Lanka had sourced bitumen from Iran, officials said, but no bitumen has arrived on regular vessels since the conflict began. The RDA has since approved bitumen from China, Thailand and European countries. Officials said its quality matches the Iranian product, but it costs more and carries higher transport charges. The price escalation has been approved for contractors. Officials said the RDA is also in talks on supply from Oman.

The RDA imports bitumen for its 10 plants and passes it on to contractors who cannot import their own. Officials put its immediate requirement at about 30,000 MT for RDA projects. With provincial road agencies included, the figure rises to about 50,000 MT. Main contractors holding Ceylon Petroleum Corporation licences have separately ordered about 20,000 MT.

“If we don’t get a solution within a month, we will have to discuss it on a Government-to-Government basis. That is the only solution,” a senior official told the committee.

Marikkar said the shortage threatened the Rs. 100 billion allocated for rural roads, which he described as the top priority. He said the Government needed a program to make full use of that money. He noted that road spending is projected at Rs. 487 billion in 2027.

He accepted that the conflict was beyond officials’ control, but said planning was also at fault. “It is true that there is a lack of planning. But if we have a plan, we can achieve more than this,” Marikkar said.

The urban development sector recorded 26% spending progress in the first 10 months of the year. The UDA itself was at 19% and forecasts just 35% by end-December. Officials blamed delays in planning projects introduced through the Budget Speech, such as the Life Cities program. They also cited slow progress on foreign-funded housing schemes financed by a bank loan and a Chinese grant, where some contracts had to be terminated and new ones signed. Contractors on the Chinese grant-funded projects have not been given price escalation, and officials said they had raised the matter with the Chinese Embassy.

The committee also directed the Ministry to wind up inactive State companies.

title: Japan eyes Sri Lanka as export manufacturing base under proposed economic corridor | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:24
-     - 14

Lanka Harness Ltd., Executive President Dr. Rohan Pallewatta (centre) explaining the manufacturing process to Japanese Ambassador Akio Isomata (left) during his visit to the factory in Biyagama yesterday

Text and pix by Charumini 

de Silva

Japan is keen to explore the proposed Japan-India-Sri Lanka economic corridor as a platform for export-oriented industrial development and regional supply chain integration, with Japanese Ambassador Akio Isomata identifying Sri Lanka’s high-value manufacturing capabilities as an important proposition.

Following a visit to Lanka Harness Ltd., at the Biyagama Export Processing Zone (EPZ) yesterday, Ambassador Isomata said he was pleased to witness company’s precision manufacturing capabilities and quality standards first-hand. He described the experience as “impressive”.

The proposed economic corridor, driven by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and the Japan External Trade Organisation (JETRO), is focused on strengthening export-oriented industrial and trade opportunities across the three countries.

Lanka Harness, which manufactures automotive electronic wire harness and critical safety components, including impact sensors for airbags and seatbelts, has established itself as a high-value export manufacturer supplying major global automotive companies. The company exports to 17 countries, including Japan, Indian China, Romania, while generating an annual revenue of over $ 80 million and providing direct and indirect employment to around 1,000 Sri Lankans.

Executive President Dr. Rohan Pallewatte said Sri Lanka has the potential to develop a $ 5 billion automotive components export industry, provided the country could offer investors policy consistency, competitive operating costs and targeted incentives to support export manufacturing.

“Attracting next wave of investment would depend on a predictable policy environment, competitive energy costs and incentives to expand manufacturing capacities,” he added.

He stressed that the proposed economic corridor could create significant opportunities for Japanese investors seeking access to India’s vast automotive supply chains, particularly under the Indo-Lanka Free Trade Agreement (FTA). 

“As the Indo-Lanka FTA qualifying products with at least 35% domestic value addition, can access preferential market entry, providing an attractive proposition for manufacturers locating production in Sri Lanka, to serve the Indian market,” he said, adding that Sri Lanka’s FTA’s with both India and Pakistan as a strategic advantage, opening access to markets representing around one-fifth of the world’s population.

Dr. Pallewatte also noted had he recently visited around 50 companies in Japan to promote Sri Lank as a manufacturing destination, noting that the country could serve as a strategic production and supply-chain hub for investors seeking access to regional markets.

He said the company had already demonstrated that Sri Lankan manufacturing talent could meet some of the world’s most demanding automotive quality requirements, maintaining a defect tolerance of just one part per million.

“What is unique is about what we do at Lanka Harness is the quality standards. The defect rate allowed is one part per million and that is the highest standard in the world,” he said, adding that sustaining such standards over decades required rigours processes and highly committed workforce.

He credited the company’s success to locally recruited employees, many drawn from villages surrounding its factories and said the workforce had consistently showcased their capability to meet demanding Japanese manufacturing standards.

Having started with an initial investment of $ 8 million in 2002, backed by a Japanese investor, Itho Yoshiyaki, despite the country’s challenging investment climate at the time, Dr. Pallewatte said Lanka Harness Ltd., has since expanded its international customer base and manufacturing capabilities.

He said the company had recently completed a new factory with available production capacity, positioning it to accommodate additional orders from Japanese manufacturers considering Sri Lanka as an export base, including companies planning to establish operations in India.

Dr. Pallewatte also noted had he recently visited around 50 companies in Japan to promote Sri Lank as a manufacturing destination, noting that the country could serve as a strategic production and supply-chain hub for investors seeking access to regional markets.

title: Listed company dividends up 12.5% to Rs. 213 b so far in 2026: CT Smith | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:23
-     - 10

Cash dividends paid by listed companies rose 12.5% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs. 213.2 billion by 19 November, up from Rs. 189.4 billion in the same period of 2025, according to CT Smith Securities.

The increase came despite fewer payouts: 206 dividends were paid by 19 November, against 211 a year earlier.

Including dividends declared for payment up to 14 December, CT Smith puts 2026 payouts so far at Rs. 241.6 billion. That is 12.1% more than the Rs. 215.6 billion paid or declared at the same point of 2025, and already 8.1% above the Rs. 223.5 billion paid in the whole of 2025.

The growth rests largely on one company. Dialog Axiata is the top payer at Rs. 33.1 billion, including Rs. 6.4 billion payable on 10 December, against Rs. 9.2 billion in 2025. Dialog raised its final dividend to Rs. 1.50 a share from Rs. 1.00 and began paying quarterly interim dividends of Rs. 0.70 a share this year. Excluding Dialog, payouts rose 1.0% to Rs. 208.5 billion from Rs. 206.4 billion at the same point of 2025.

Ceylon Tobacco Company is the second-largest payer at Rs. 30.3 billion, including Rs. 7.7 billion payable on 11 December, followed by Commercial Bank at Rs. 13.1 billion, Sampath Bank at Rs. 12.1 billion, Distilleries Company of Sri Lanka at Rs. 9.2 billion, Hatton National Bank at Rs. 8.6 billion and Melstacorp at Rs. 7.0 billion. Together, the seven account for Rs. 113.3 billion, or 47% of the total.

By sector, Food, Beverage and Tobacco led payouts, followed by Banks, Telecoms, Capital Goods, Diversified Financials, Materials and Insurance.

Dividends are also concentrated among fewer companies. The number of companies paying fell 9.7% to 139 from 154, and the number of dividends fell 3.8% to 228 from 237 at the same point of 2025.


By quarter, payouts rose 28.0% YoY to Rs. 46.3 billion in the first quarter, 6.1% to Rs. 82.9 billion in the second and 24.4% to Rs. 77.5 billion in the third. Fourth-quarter payouts paid and declared so far stand at Rs. 35.0 billion, against Rs. 39.1 billion at the same point of 2025 and Rs. 46.9 billion for the whole of the fourth quarter of 2025.

The payouts come against modest earnings growth. Corporate earnings of companies listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange rose 10% YoY to Rs. 168.3 billion in the second quarter of 2026, led by the banking sector. That lifted cumulative earnings for the first half of 2026 to Rs. 354.9 billion, an 8% increase YoY. Full-year earnings were Rs. 685.3 billion in 2025 and Rs. 672.4 billion in 2024.

CT Smith Securities Associate Vice President – Research Kasun Herath said underlying dividend growth remains broad, with 76 of the 127 companies that paid in both years increasing payouts, against 30 that reduced them.

“The drag comes from 27 companies that had paid or declared Rs. 24.5 billion by this point last year but have declared no cash dividend so far this year. The decline is concentrated in diversified financials, where payouts are down ~40%, while five companies have opted for scrip dividends instead of cash,” Herath said.

“Dialog’s increase is also partly timing-related, with 2026 carrying both its final dividend for 2025 and three interim dividends for 2026 following its shift to quarterly payouts. This makes growth next year less likely to be driven by Dialog and more dependent on the broader market,” he said.

title: NSB Group delivers Rs. 45.8 b operating profit in 9M | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:22
-     - 11

National Savings Bank Group (NSB) yesterday said it has sustained its core banking momentum during the first nine months of 2026, supported by stronger net interest income, strong growth in fee-based earnings and continued expansion in loans and advances.

The Group’s net interest income rose 7.4% to Rs. 69.1 billion, total operating income increased 3.6% to Rs. 71.2 billion and net operating income grew 5.4% to Rs. 75.3 billion. Group profit before tax amounted to Rs. 34.7 billion, broadly in line with Rs. 34.8 billion in the corresponding period of 2025, while profit after tax stood at Rs. 20.7 billion. Group total assets increased to Rs. 1.92 trillion and Group equity rose 8.7% to Rs. 139.05 billion.

The Bank reported total operating income of Rs. 69.8 billion for the period, an increase of 4.6% compared with Rs. 66.7 billion in the corresponding period of 2025. Net operating income increased by 6.4% to Rs. 73.9 billion from Rs. 69.4 billion a year ago, supported by a net impairment reversal of Rs. 4.1 billion arising from improved recoveries and asset quality.

Net interest income rose by 6.4% year-on-year to Rs. 67.3 billion, compared with Rs. 63.2 billion in the first nine months of 2025. Interest income increased 1.8% to Rs. 150.8 billion, while interest expenses declined 1.6% to Rs. 83.5 billion. The result reflects strict financial discipline, prudent balance-sheet management and the Bank’s continued focus on maintaining a sustainable funding and asset mix.

The Bank also achieved substantial growth in fee-based earnings. Fee and commission income rose 32.1% to Rs. 2.58 billion, and net fee and commission income increased by 34.2% to Rs. 2.21 billion, from Rs. 1.65 billion a year earlier. Net other operating income increased 53.2% to Rs. 924 million. These gains were partly offset by a net trading loss of Rs. 744 million, compared with a trading gain of Rs. 775 million in the previous year.

Profit before tax amounted to Rs. 33.7 billion, an increase of 1.1% from Rs. 33.3 billion in the first nine months of 2025, while profit after tax stood at Rs. 20 billion, compared with Rs. 20.11 billion.

Despite these pressures, the Bank preserved a substantial earnings base and continued to invest in the people, systems and service capabilities required to improve operational resilience and the customer experience. Income tax for the period amounted to Rs. 13.7 billion, while VAT and the Social Security Contribution Levy on financial services together amounted to Rs. 10.9 billion. In addition, the Bank declared a dividend of Rs. 7.4 billion to the Government as its sole shareholder. Accordingly, NSB’s total contribution to the Government through dividends, taxes and levies amounted to Rs. 32 billion for the nine months, underscoring the Bank’s significant contribution to public finances and national development.

Chairman Dr. Harsha Cabral, PC said: “Our nine-month results reflect the resilience of NSB’s core business and the trust placed in the Bank by generations of Sri Lankans. While expanding lending and improving asset quality, we remain focused on the prudent stewardship of public savings and on supporting productive economic activity, financial inclusion and national development.”

NSB’s total assets increased by 2.6% during the first nine months of the year to Rs. 1.88 trillion, from Rs. 1.83 trillion at end-December 2025. Loans and advances recorded a strong 11.3% expansion to Rs. 613.1 billion from Rs. 550.8 billion, demonstrating the Bank’s continued support for the financing needs of individuals, households and eligible institutional customers within its mandate.

Deposits, the principal source of funding for NSB, increased by 1.9% to Rs. 1.64 trillion from Rs. 1.61 trillion. The Bank’s financial position remained sound, with total shareholders’ equity increasing by 9.0% to Rs. 129.7 billion from Rs. 119.1 billion. Retained earnings rose by 14.7% to Rs. 53.41 billion, further strengthening the Bank’s capacity to support future growth and absorb potential shocks.

General Manager/CEO Rohana Bandara Weerakoon said: “The growth we have achieved in lending, savings, foreign currency deposits and fee income shows the progress we are making in diversifying our business. We will continue to strengthen digital access, service quality, cost discipline and risk management while delivering on NSB’s national mandate.”

The Bank’s profitability indicators continued to reflect the strength of its core banking activities, although higher operating expenses moderated overall returns. The Net Interest Margin (NIM) improved to 4.85% from 4.74% at the end of 2025. Return on Assets (ROA) remained broadly stable at 2.43%, compared with 2.48%, while Return on Equity (ROE) stood at 21.49%, compared with 25.08% at the end of 2025.

Asset quality continued to improve. The net Stage 3 loans ratio improved to 2.00% from 2.52%. At the same time, the Stage 3 impairment coverage ratio strengthened to 59.42% from 58.54%, reflecting improved coverage against Stage 3 loans.

NSB maintained capital buffers comfortably above the applicable regulatory minimum requirements. The Tier 1 capital ratio stood at 18.23% against a minimum of 8.5%, and the total capital ratio at 19.43%, well above the minimum requirement of 12.5%.

The Bank also maintained a strong liquidity and stable funding position. The all-currency liquidity coverage ratio stood at 307.17%, substantially above the statutory minimum of 100%, reflecting the availability of sufficient high-quality liquid assets to meet short-term liquidity requirements. The net stable funding ratio stood at 195.60%, also comfortably above the regulatory minimum of 100%, demonstrating the stability of the Bank’s longer-term funding profile.

title: Saudi Prince prevails in high-profile film dispute in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:21
-     - 12

Prince Al Waleed bin Talal bin Abdulaziz Al Saud

A long-running legal battle involving a proposed international film project came to a close on 16 October 2026, when Sri Lanka’s Supreme Court ruled in favour of His Royal Highness Prince Al Waleed Bin Talal Bin Abdul Aziz Al Saud. 

The judgment brought an end to a claim pursued by M.Z.M. Rafick, a film writer, promoter and producer operating under the name Puma International. The Prince was represented by Avindra Rodrigo, President’s Counsel, on the instructions of F J & G de Saram.

The dispute stemmed from a film concept titled ‘The Diamond Merchant’, a story set against the backdrop of the Bosnian conflict and intended to promote understanding between Christian and Muslim communities. 

According to Rafick, he met the Prince at a Colombo hotel in March 2005 and presented the storyline. He claimed that the Prince was sufficiently impressed by the concept to enter into an oral agreement to produce the film once the script was further developed. When the project never materialised, Rafick commenced legal proceedings, alleging a breach of that agreement. 

However, the Courts found that the evidence did not support the existence of the alleged agreement. The Commercial High Court had previously dismissed the action in 2019, concluding that Rafick had failed to prove that any oral agreement had been reached and that there was no basis for the intellectual property claims that accompanied the case. 

On appeal, the Supreme Court undertook a detailed examination of the legal principles governing oral contracts. While reaffirming that oral agreements are recognised under both Roman-Dutch and English law, and by Sri Lankan Courts, the Supreme Court emphasised a fundamental principle; a party alleging the existence of an oral agreement bears the burden of proving it. 

In this case, the Court concluded that the evidence fell short of establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that such an agreement had ever been concluded. 

The Court ultimately affirmed the Commercial High Court’s decision and held that no oral agreement existed between Rafick and the Prince. It also observed that, in light of the concessions made during the proceedings, there was no need to issue separate declaratory relief in relation to the intellectual property rights claimed over ‘The Diamond Merchant’. 

Beyond its high-profile parties and cinematic backdrop, the decision serves as a timely reminder of the challenges involved in proving oral agreements. The judgment reinforces the importance of clear evidence when parties seek to establish contractual rights arising from conversations and understandings that were never reduced to writing.

Avindra Rodrigo, PC with Christina Hettiarachchi and Hashendra Jayasuriya instructed by FJ&G de Saram appeared for the Prince, while Roshan Hettiarachchi instructed by Kalindi Silva appeared for M.Z.M. Rafick.

title: Developing countries’ external debt surges to record $ 9.4 t | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:20
-     - 10

External debt of developing countries jumped 5.5% to a record $ 9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest pace since 2021 and about four times the 2022–24 average, according to the World Bank Group’s International Debt Report 2026. 

Access to international finance has improved, but the price of finance has not, and high debt burdens in the poorest countries threaten to crowd out essential investments in people.

Private financing drove much of the increase. Borrowing from private creditors jumped and bond issuance from public entities rose nearly 35% to $ 251 billion, the highest level in five years as markets reopened to many developing countries. External debt grew fastest among the most vulnerable countries, increasing 8.1% to $ 1.3 trillion in countries eligible for concessional financing from the World Bank Group’s International Development Association (IDA).

World Bank Group Chief Statistician and Director of Development Data Haishan Fu said:  “The return of private lending to low- and middle-income countries is welcome, but these countries are borrowing more, paying more, and in many cases leaving less for long-term development. Managing debt responsibly means giving everyone—including future generations—a chance to thrive.”

Many governments issued new Bonds to buy back maturing debt, smoothing repayment profiles without significantly reducing debt stocks, often at higher interest rates. Early 2026 data show continued demand for international bond financing from low- and middle-income countries despite the high costs. By mid-August, more than 10 countries had exceeded their full-year 2025 issuance, while several others returned to international markets.

IDA-eligible countries paid an average of 8.2% on new private-creditor commitments in 2025—the highest rate since 1989—and 9.4% on new Bonds. The gap between the rates IDA-eligible countries paid to official and private creditors widened from 3.4 percentage points in 2016 to 5.5 percentage points in 2025.

In comparison, countries eligible for only non-concessional loans from the World Bank Group’s International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD) paid an average of 5.5% on new Bonds, an improvement from the 5.8% rate the previous year.

Debt-service pressures remained severe amid elevated global interest rates. Low- and middle-income countries paid $ 1.4 trillion in principal and interest in 2025, up 1.9% and marking a fifth consecutive annual increase. Payments to bondholders climbed to $ 363 billion, partly reflecting debt buybacks and prepayments financed through new Bond issues.

Between 2022 through 2025, developing countries paid $ 436 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing. The direction shifted in 2025, however, as long-term debt flows turned from a $ 118 billion net outflow in 2024 to a net inflow of $ 45 billion.

Currency movements also played a role in the reported increase. More than a quarter of the $ 303 billion increase in public and publicly guaranteed debt reflected the weaker US dollar, which raised the dollar value of debt denominated in other currencies. For several of the largest concessional borrowers, these currency effects outweighed the principal they repaid in 2025, leaving reported debt higher despite continued servicing.

title: Uber backs Sri Lanka’s next wave of tech entrepreneurs | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:04
-     - 11

Uber, recently announced the winners of Uber Springboard 2026, its annual mentorship initiative supporting Sri Lanka’s emerging entrepreneurs. 

Selected from a record 150 applications this year, winning start-ups Thingsnode, MonChron and NeuroFleets will now receive hands-on mentorship from senior Uber technology and business leaders at the company’s Tech Centre of Excellence in Hyderabad, India.

Now in its third edition, Uber Springboard continues to serve as a platform connecting promising Sri Lankan startups with global technology expertise. Organised in collaboration with the Ministry of Digital Economy, Government of Sri Lanka, the initiative offers founders practical guidance on product development, technology, business strategy and scaling operations. This year’s winners are working across clean energy, artificial intelligence and logistics, demonstrating how Sri Lankan innovation is addressing challenges with relevance far beyond the island.

Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne said: “Sri Lanka’s digital economy will be shaped by entrepreneurs who can turn bold ideas into globally competitive businesses. Our role is to help create the ecosystem for that ambition to succeed, including access to technology, expertise and international networks. The record 150 applications to Uber Springboard this year are an encouraging sign of the innovation and enterprise emerging from Sri Lanka. I congratulate the three winning startups and commend Uber for its continued commitment to nurturing Sri Lankan talent and helping our entrepreneurs realise their global ambitions.”

Uber Springboard 2026 winners

Thingsnode, founded by Migara Amithodhana, is helping make renewable energy operations smarter through technology that monitors and optimises clean-energy assets. Its solutions already support over 500 MW of renewable energy capacity.

MonChron, founded by 18-year-old Ganidhu Kandepola, is reimagining video editing with an AI-powered tool that allows content creators worldwide to automate complex post-production tasks through simple conversations.

NeuroFleets, a Jaffna-based startup co-founded by Lavanya Ratanbala and Robinroy Peter, is using edge AI and autonomous hardware to coordinate logistics fleets and eliminate downtime in third-party logistics warehouses.

Uber Sri Lanka Country Manager – Delivery Varun Wijewardane said: “What stands out about this year’s winners is the future-facing sectors they represent - from artificial intelligence and autonomous technology to clean energy. It is equally encouraging to see innovation emerging from beyond Colombo, reflecting the depth of entrepreneurial talent across Sri Lanka. Through Springboard, we remain committed to nurturing this talent, sharing Uber’s global expertise and helping promising startups build businesses that can scale in Sri Lanka and beyond.”

Uber Sri Lanka Country Manager – Mobility Kaushalya Gunaratne said: “When an 18-year-old entrepreneur is already building technology for a global audience, it says something about the ambition and potential of Sri Lanka’s next generation of innovators. Great ideas can come from anywhere, but turning them into successful businesses takes the right guidance and opportunity. We’re proud to play a part in that journey and grateful to the Ministry of Digital Economy for partnering with us to help Sri Lankan entrepreneurs turn their ideas into innovations that can make an impact at home and globally.”

The selected start-up founders will participate in structured mentorship sessions at Uber’s Hyderabad Tech Centre, engaging with senior leaders on product development, technology and business growth. The third edition builds on Springboard’s 2024 and 2025 programmes, reinforcing Uber’s broader contribution to Sri Lanka’s digital economy beyond its mobility and delivery businesses.

title: ‘Aiming to create generation of Sri Lankans with entrepreneurial mindset’ | Daily FT
summary:

title: National policy framework for data centres and cloud infrastructure taking shape | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:01
-     - 7

The Board of Investment of Sri Lanka (BOI), together with the Ministry of Digital Economy (MoDE) and GovTech Sri Lanka, has taken a decisive step towards establishing a national investment strategy for data centres, convening a National Stakeholder Consultation on the National Policy Framework for Data Centre and Cloud Infrastructure Investment on 6 November, 2026.

Co-chaired by BOI Chairman Duminda Hulangamuwa and Chief Advisor to the President on Digital Economy Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya, with the participation of BOI Director General Dr. Sulakshana Jayawardena, the consultation brought together close to 40 senior representatives from the institutions that will underpin the sector. These included the Ministry of Energy, the Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development, the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka, the Telecommunications Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka, the National System Operator Ltd., Electricity Distribution Lanka Ltd., the National Transmission Network Service Provider Ltd., the National Water Supply and Drainage Board, the Central Environmental Authority and the Sri Lanka Sustainable Energy Authority.

The session marked the final stage of consensus-building on the core investment parameters for the sector, namely electricity tariffs, land and water allocations, connectivity requirements, access to renewable energy and fiscal incentives, while also confirming the readiness of zone infrastructure and the responsibilities of each institution.

Building on extensive groundwork

The consultation follows several months of structured preparation. This included the establishment of a Steering Committee, a market-sounding Request for Information (RFI) that attracted more than 30 responses from industry, a series of technical consultations, and an expert assessment by global consultancy Roland Berger, undertaken with technical assistance from the Asian Development Bank (ADB). In parallel, the BOI has continued its direct engagement with prospective investors.

Opening the proceedings, Hulangamuwa outlined the joint BOI–MoDE initiative to position Sri Lanka as a competitive destination for data centre investment. Dr. Wijayasuriya highlighted the potential of the sector both to accelerate domestic digitalisation and to open new export opportunities, while emphasising that, given the central role of electricity, the industry should be developed in a measured and sustainable manner.

A clear national ambition

Participants reviewed the proposed national capacity targets of 25 MW by 2027 and 50 MW by 2028, with an indicative mix of 75% conventional compute and 25% AI compute, and an ambition to attract hyperscale data centre investments. Proposed investment terms were presented for both grid-supplied and renewable-integrated data centres, covering greenfield projects as well as expansions.

Stakeholders proposed several refinements to strengthen the framework, including:

Investment-ready locations

Dr. Jayawardena presented preliminary investment locations within BOI zones, comprising both grid-supplied sites and captive-power, renewable-integrated sites. The BOI will now work with the relevant utility and regulatory agencies to document site-specific infrastructure availability and readiness before the investment locations are formally published, ensuring that investors receive accurate, decision-ready information.

The road ahead

The Ministry of Digital Economy will revise the proposed Data Centre Investment Terms to reflect stakeholder feedback, and the BOI will convene a second stakeholder meeting in December 2026 to resolve outstanding matters and finalise the terms. Approval for a dedicated data centre electricity tariff framework is also being pursued, with the aim of completing the policy package by the end of the year.

The finalised framework is expected to give local and international investors a transparent, coordinated pathway to establish data centre and cloud infrastructure in Sri Lanka, supporting the country’s digital economy ambitions and its broader drive to attract high-value foreign direct investment.

title: Sri Lanka launches Marine Industries Advisory Committee to position country as regional maritime hub | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:00
-     - 10

The inaugural meeting of the Advisory Committee on Marine-Based Industries was held on 16 November 2026 at the Sri Lanka Export Development Board (EDB), bringing together key public and private sector stakeholders to discuss strategic priorities, industry challenges and emerging opportunities for the development of Sri Lanka’s marine-based industries.

The meeting was attended by the EDB Chairman, Director General, and the Additional Director General (Development), underscoring the importance placed on the sector as a key component of Sri Lanka’s export diversification and economic growth agenda.

During the meeting, Kaushal Rajapaksa was appointed as Chairman of the Marine-Based Services Advisory Committee, while Ricky Barnett was appointed as Co-Chairman. Members expressed confidence in their leadership to drive the Committee’s future initiatives and strengthen collaboration among industry stakeholders.

EDB Chairman Mangala Wijesinghe delivered the main presentation, outlining the current status of the sector, emerging global opportunities, and the strategic priorities required to position Sri Lanka as a competitive regional hub for marine-based services. The presentation highlighted the sector’s growth potential and the need for coordinated efforts to enhance value addition, innovation, skills development, and international market access.

The Committee members actively contributed to the discussions by sharing ideas, perspectives, and strategic recommendations for sector development. A key area of discussion was the need to address infrastructure and space constraints affecting the expansion of shipbuilding, ship repair and vessel conversion activities. Industry representatives highlighted the limited availability of suitable industrial space within the Colombo Port for fabrication, vessel construction, assembly, storage, equipment installation and sea trials. The importance of identifying suitable alternative locations and developing dedicated industrial facilities to accommodate the industry’s future requirements was emphasised.

The Committee also discussed opportunities to strengthen marine infrastructure and tourism-related activities, including the development of marinas, sheltered anchorages, breakwaters, boatyards and other marine tourism facilities. The potential to develop existing harbors, including Galle and other coastal locations, as marine tourism and boating hubs was highlighted. In this regard, the progress of the proposed Kapparathota Marina Development Project was discussed.

Another important area of discussion was the taxation structure and HS Code classification applicable to locally manufactured commercial boats supplied to domestic tourism operators. The Committee also emphasised the importance of fostering stronger public-private partnerships (PPPs) and creating an enabling environment that supports sustainable growth and increased export earnings from marine-based services.

Speaking at the meeting, Committee Chair Rajapaksa noted the significant opportunities available within the sector and stressed the importance of collective action to unlock its full potential. Some members of the committee highlighted the need for continuous engagement with industry stakeholders to ensure that the Committee’s recommendations translate into tangible outcomes.

To facilitate focused discussions and effective implementation of proposed initiatives, the establishment of specialised subcommittees covering Boat Building and Manufacturing, Shipbuilding and Ship Repair, Regulatory Affairs, Training and Skills Development, Marketing and Export Promotion, Nautical and Marine Tourism, and Offshore Services was discussed. These subcommittees are expected to develop practical proposals and recommendations addressing specific industry requirements.

The Committee also highlighted the opportunities presented by Sri Lanka Expo 2027, particularly in promoting marine-related investment opportunities, showcasing industry capabilities and connecting local businesses with international buyers and investors. Members were encouraged to identify potential buyers, investors and investment-ready marine-related projects for promotion at the event. The importance of aligning the Committee’s activities with the National Export Development Plan (2026–2030) and strengthening coordination among relevant government institutions was also emphasised.

The inaugural meeting concluded with a shared commitment to translate the discussions and recommendations into practical initiatives, with an emphasis on measurable outcomes, effective implementation and collaborative actions among industry stakeholders and government institutions.

The establishment of the Marine-Based Services Advisory Committee marks an important step towards strengthening Sri Lanka’s blue economy and leveraging the country’s strategic maritime location to generate sustainable economic growth and export-led development.

title: Govt. to evaluate BOI, SDP and Port City tax incentives | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:00
-     - 9

The Government has begun cost-benefit reviews of tax incentives granted to Board of Investment (BOI) Strategic Development Projects (SDPs) and Colombo Port City businesses, as Corporate Income Tax (CIT) reliefs for BOI enterprises climbed 54% in 2024/25.

According to the Finance Ministry’s Tax Expenditure Statement 2025/2026 released on 12 November 2026, CIT reliefs for BOI companies rose to Rs. 65 billion in 2024/25 from Rs. 42 billion in 2023/24. Exemptions for non-SDP BOI companies, which were nil the previous year, amounted to Rs. 53 billion. Concessionary rates for these companies fell to Rs. 11.5 billion from Rs. 41.7 billion.

SDPs accounted for Rs. 84 million in concessionary-rate CIT relief in 2024/25, compared with Rs. 123 million in exemptions the previous year. Port City projects received no CIT relief in 2024/25, after Rs. 143 million in exemptions in 2023/24.

BOI companies also received Rs. 28.1 billion in Value Added Tax (VAT) relief and Rs. 15.8 billion in Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL) relief in 2025, a combined Rs. 43.9 billion. In the first half of 2026 they received Rs. 18.9 billion in VAT relief and Rs. 10.1 billion in SSCL relief. Other manufacturing activities led BOI VAT reliefs in 2025 at Rs. 15.7 billion, followed by wholesale and retail at Rs. 9.3 billion. Textiles and garments led BOI SSCL reliefs at Rs. 5.9 billion.

SDPs received Rs. 286 million in VAT relief in 2025, almost all of it in tourism, and Rs. 93 million in SSCL relief. Port City projects received Rs. 11 million in SSCL relief in 2025 and Rs. 13 million in the first half of 2026.

The Port City duty-free shop recorded the sharpest rise. Its Customs Import Duty relief rose to Rs. 757 million in 2025 from Rs. 46 million in 2024, and reached Rs. 456 million in the first half of 2026. Its excise relief, however, fell to Rs. 94 million from Rs. 250 million.

The Ministry expects these costs to grow. “Tax expenditure associated with Port City projects is expected to increase over the medium term as approved businesses commence operations and become eligible for incentives provided under the relevant legislative framework,” the statement said.

To keep the cost in check, the Ministry has introduced ex-ante cost-benefit analyses and ex-post evaluations of incentives granted to SDPs, and technical analyses and ex-post evaluations of incentives granted under the Colombo Port City Economic Commission. “The Strategic Development Projects (Amendment) Act, No. 26 of 2025, and the Colombo Port City Economic Commission (Amendment) Act, No. 1 of 2026, have strengthened the tax incentive framework by providing for specified periods for the granting of tax incentives,” it said.

The Ministry cautioned that the final bill for large projects is uncertain. “For major investment projects, including BOI projects, Strategic Development Projects, and Colombo Port City projects, the actual fiscal cost may depend on the implementation of investment commitments and the achievement of employment, production, export and other project outcomes,” it said.

title: Australian envoy highlights investment, development partnerships | Daily FT

Australian High Commissioner to Sri Lanka Matthew Duckworth yesterday briefed senior editors from leading Sri Lankan media houses on Australia’s diplomatic priorities and bilateral initiatives, ahead of the 80th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the two countries next year.

The briefing was organised by the OzLanka Journalists’ Consortium in partnership with Australia’s Market Development Facility (MDF). Discussions covered Australian investment, development partnerships and Australia’s contribution to Sri Lanka’s economic growth.

“Australia deeply values our longstanding partnership with Sri Lanka, and next year marks 80 years of our bilateral relations,” Duckworth said. “We take this very seriously and look forward to telling this story more broadly next year. As neighbours in this region, we recognise each other as long-term partners and friends, and we want to continue supporting and building upon these ties.”

The High Commissioner also reaffirmed Australia’s support for press freedom and regional media cooperation.

“We value independent and credible journalism as a public good. Therefore, we are committed to engaging with you regularly and operating as openly and transparently as possible,” he said.

He pointed to the recently launched “Digital Turtles” program and exchange visits for media representatives as evidence of Canberra’s commitment to skills development, information sharing and stronger ties between the two countries’ media sectors.

MDF Sri Lanka Country Director Maryam Piracha outlined the work of the Australian Government-funded program, which has operated in the country since 2015. MDF co-invests with private sector firms to promote sustainable, inclusive growth in high-value, export-oriented sectors, including tourism, specialty coffee and agriculture.

“MDF is committed to building partnerships that enhance competitiveness, drive economic diversification, and create inclusive opportunities, particularly for women and smallholder farmers across Sri Lanka’s key value chains, in both agriculture and tourism,” Piracha said.

The event also saw the launch of the OzLanka Media Forum, a platform created to open direct dialogue between the Australian High Commissioner and local journalists on developments in the bilateral relationship.

OzLanka Journalists’ Consortium President Claude Gunasekara welcomed the initiative and said he hoped the forum would help deepen bilateral understanding and engagement through Sri Lanka’s media.

Duckworth thanked the participating journalists and said he looked forward to further collaboration.

title: Morison embarks on exports journey with medical marketing operations in Cambodia | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:00
-     - 8

Morison, a pioneer in Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturing with over 60 years of industrial expertise and a member of the Hemas Group, recently embarked on its landmark exports journey, establishing its own medical marketing operations in Cambodia. 

The first export consignment was shipped to the country on 11 November, 2026, marking a significant milestone and a historic first in the company’s journey of taking home-grown pharmaceuticals to the world.

The endeavour distinguishes Morison as the first Sri Lankan pharma manufacturer to initiate medical marketing operations in a foreign country through its own team of medical representatives. Headed by a Sri Lankan country manager, Morison has already secured 13 product registrations in Cambodia, with another seven currently in the process of being approved.

Reflecting on the significance of this milestone for the Group, Hemas Healthcare Cluster Chairman Murtaza Esufally said: “For the past 70 years, Hemas has been importing pharmaceuticals to Sri Lanka. Therefore, witnessing Hemas-manufactured pharmaceuticals being exported to another country for the first time is a particularly proud moment for us. It marks a significant milestone in our journey and reflects our ambition to take Sri Lankan pharmaceutical manufacturing beyond our shores.”

The inaugural shipment comprised three of Morison’s newly launched niche, novel therapies, carrying the same brand names under which they are marketed in Sri Lanka: EmpaMor (Empagliflozin Tablets 10 mg and 25 mg), BisoMor (Bisoprolol Tablets BP 2.5 mg and 5 mg) and RivoMor (Rivaroxaban Tablets 10 mg and 20 mg).

Speaking on what this milestone means for Morison’s future, Morison Ltd Managing Director Dinesh Athapaththu said: “This milestone marks a significant achievement for Morison. Initiating our first export shipment and launching our very own medical marketing operation in Cambodia is just the commencement of turning a much bigger, long-term exports roadmap into a reality.”

Cambodia’s market of approximately 18 million people is currently valued at nearly $ 350 million and depends on imports for nearly 95% of its pharmaceutical needs. The country operates in line with WHO GMP guidelines, making it a natural first destination for medicines manufactured to international standards in Sri Lanka.

The timing of the first shipment also carries a special significance for Morison. Exactly four years ago, on 11 November, 2022, the company announced its entry into the branded generics space in Sri Lanka, making 11 November a special day in the Morison calendar.

Leading the Cambodian operations as Country Manager is Prabuddha Walpita, previously Senior Manager Commercial at Morison. Having been with the company for the last 10 years, he has built his career at Morison, rising through the ranks across a variety of roles.

Commenting on his appointment, Walpita said: “Having joined Morison as a fresh graduate back in 2016, over the last 10 years I have seen the company transition from the home of Morison’s Gripe Mixture and Morison’s Lacto Calamine to a respected branded generics pharma manufacturer among the medical fraternity, and now to one that is expanding its horizons to the global market. I am truly grateful to have been entrusted with this new challenge. I am excited to take our own pharma brands, built right here in Sri Lanka, to the Cambodian market, navigating any challenges that may come along the way.”

Having entered the branded generics segment just four years ago, the company has already made a significant footprint in the diabetes space, with EmpaMor becoming the highest-selling empagliflozin brand within two years of its launch. Morison has since expanded into cardiovascular products, where it continues to gain traction, supported by its new state-of-the-art pharmaceutical manufacturing facility in Homagama.

title: Eight EPDP members sentenced to death for 2008 murder | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 20 November 2026 00:02
-     - 8

The Batticaloa High Court yesterday sentenced eight members of the Eelam People’s Democratic Party (EPDP) to death for the abduction and murder of a man in Eravur, Batticaloa, in 2008, during the civil war.

The court found the eight guilty of unlawful assembly and the murder of Devadas Suresh Kumar. It acquitted and released a ninth accused.

Suresh Kumar was abducted on 19 June, 2008, reportedly taken away in a van by a group of EPDP members attached to a camp in Chenkalady. According to evidence presented at the trial, he was murdered and buried, with a banana sapling planted over the burial site.

Eravur Police arrested nine EPDP members and filed proceedings in the Batticaloa Magistrate’s Court. Investigators also recovered the van allegedly used in the abduction. The case was transferred to the High Court in 2016.

In addition to the death sentences, the eight were given six months’ simple imprisonment under Section 140 of the Penal Code for being members of an unlawful assembly with the common object of committing murder. They were then taken to Batticaloa Prison.
